t.2.90.2: Meanwhile, frightened and distressed by that great noise, the rutting leaders of the herds fled with their herds in all directions.
t.2.90.1: As he sat there thus, the dust and the din of the army of the approaching Bharata rose up, both reaching to the sky.
t.2.90.3: Rāghava heard that sound arising from the army, and he looked upon all those leaders of the herds as they fled in every direction.
t.2.90.4: Seeing them fleeing and hearing that tumult, Rāma spoke to Saumitri Lakṣmaṇa of blazing splendor.
t.2.90.6: Is it a king, or one equal to a king, roaming the forest on a hunt, or is it some wild beast? Saumitri, you should find out. You should learn the truth of all this without delay.
t.2.90.5: Ah, Lakṣmaṇa, look here! Through you Sumitrā is blessed with a noble son. A tumultuous sound is heard, deep as fearsome thunder.
t.2.90.7: Lakṣmaṇa, in great haste, climbed a flowering sāla tree and, scanning all the directions, looked toward the eastern quarter.
t.2.90.8: Facing north and gazing out, he saw a vast army crowded with chariots, horses and elephants, and furnished with alert, ready foot-soldiers.
t.2.90.9: He told Rāma of that army, filled with horses and elephants and adorned with chariots and banners, and spoke these words.
t.2.90.11: Rāma, the tiger among men, replied to Lakṣmaṇa: "Look carefully, Saumitri! Whose army do you think this is?"
t.2.90.10: Let the noble one put out the fire, and let Sītā take refuge in the cave. String your bow, and make ready your arrows and your armour as well.
t.2.90.12: Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words, enraged like a blazing fire, as though wishing to burn up that army.
t.2.90.14: Indeed, this very great and splendid tree shines brightly; on the chariot gleams the banner bearing the kovidāra, its trunk rising high.
t.2.90.13: Having obtained the consecration and wishing for a secure kingdom, Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, is clearly coming to kill us both.
t.2.90.15: These men, mounting swift-going horses, ride about as they please; and these riders, delighted, shine forth as they sit mounted upon elephants.
t.2.90.16: Bows in hand, O hero, we two take our stand upon the mountain; perhaps he whose banner bears the kovidāra tree may yet fall into our power in battle.
t.2.90.17: Shall I at last see Bharata, on whose account this great calamity has befallen you, O Rāghava, and Sītā and me as well?
t.2.90.18: O Rāghava, Bharata, the one on whose account you have fallen from the everlasting kingdom, has arrived. This enemy, O hero, must surely be slain by me.
t.2.90.19: I see no wrong in slaying Bharata, O Rāghava, for no unrighteousness is incurred in casting off those who have done harm before. When he has been slain, rule over the whole earth.
t.2.90.20: Today may Kaikeyī, greedy for the kingdom, deeply stricken with grief, behold her son slain by me in battle, like a tree broken by an elephant.
t.2.90.21: I shall slay Kaikeyī too, together with her followers and her kinsmen; today let the earth be freed from this great sin.
t.2.90.22: Today, O bestower of honor, I shall loose this long-restrained anger and the insult we have suffered upon the enemy's hosts, as one lets fire loose upon dry brushwood.
t.2.90.23: Today, piercing the bodies of the enemies with sharpened arrows, I shall make this forest of Citrakūṭa drenched with blood.
t.2.90.24: Let the beasts of prey drag about the elephants and horses, their hearts pierced by my arrows, and the men slain by me.
t.2.90.25: Here in the great forest I will be free of my debt to my arrows and my bow; having slain Bharata together with his army, so I shall be, there is no doubt.
